note: Assumptions that are ours, not a publisher's. Each states its basis and which way it biases the result.

assumptions.assumption: Kosovo (XK) is in the network topology but carries no demand or generation weights, so no transfer pattern sources, sinks or crosses it and it has no register or planned branches.
assumptions.basis: The TYNDP 2026 scenario tables this screen is shaped by publish no XK figures (every other Balkan system is present). Inventing weights would breach the provenance rule: a value is sourced, inferred or unknown.
assumptions.bias: Kosovan branches appear only as unexposed or under other systems' transfers; Kosovan stress is UNDERSTATED. Plugging this needs a sourced demand/generation figure (e.g. KOSTT adequacy data), not a guess.

assumptions.assumption: The 'with plans' network only contains what a source publishes: national register schemes where a TSO plan was harvested, TYNDP projects everywhere, RTE/NVE geometry for France/Norway. Several countries have no harvested national plan and therefore contribute only TYNDP-level projects.
assumptions.basis: Plan harvesting is per-source manual work; the public map's coverage note names the worst gaps (Greece, Croatia, Lithuania, Belgium regional plans, Italy's unplaceable interventions).
assumptions.bias: Plan relief is understated in un-harvested countries, so their residual 'with plans' stress reads HIGH relative to well-harvested neighbours. Cross-country plan-effect comparisons are only meaningful between well-covered countries.

assumptions.assumption: A planned AC branch may not join two synchronous areas. Candidate terminal pairings that cross one are rejected and the circuit's full rating is renormalised onto the pairings that remain.
assumptions.basis: Ireland, GB, the Nordic area and Continental Europe are coupled only by HVDC. An AC branch across one of those interfaces fuses two areas into a single connected component and rewrites the PTDFs of everything in both. Three real schemes were doing this before the guard.
assumptions.bias: A scheme whose every pairing crosses is dropped, which understates plan relief for that scheme. Counted as area_repair_failed.

assumptions.assumption: Stations whose recorded name is the literal string 'unknown' take no part in name matching.
assumptions.basis: 5,175 of 29,063 substations (18%) carry that placeholder, all normalising to one token, so any endpoint text drifting towards it could match an arbitrary one of them anywhere in Europe. The provenance rule forbids turning an unknown into a plausible value. They remain available as geometric terminals.
assumptions.bias: 18 schemes that previously entered the model on an arbitrary busbar no longer enter as branches. Understates plan relief; the alternative was a wrong circuit.

assumptions.assumption: An endpoint may match a station in another country only if the two share a land border and the normalised text is at least four characters.
assumptions.basis: Genuine interconnector schemes name a station across the border, so the path is needed. Unconstrained it accepted any globally unique name: 'M50 [sheet 1-TID r327]' reduced to 'm', matched Swiss station M07 and drew a Dublin ducting project as a 1,295 km Alps-to-Ireland line at match score 100.
assumptions.bias: None known. Every real interconnector in the register still matches.

assumptions.assumption: A scheme's two endpoints may not be further apart than the ceiling for its voltage class (250/285/520/730/1080 km for the 90-149/150-219/220-349/350-499/500+ kV classes). Beyond it the weaker-scored endpoint is discarded and the scheme keeps only its better-matched end.
assumptions.basis: Derived from this dataset's own existing network - the 99.9th-percentile single-span route length per class, tripled to allow a genuine multi-span corridor. A name match can be wrong INSIDE one country, where the adjacency rule cannot help: 'Coslada - Villaverde Bajo 220 kV' (both in Madrid) was drawn 1,582 km long.
assumptions.bias: A genuinely long domestic corridor loses one endpoint and is modelled as a point. Understates plan relief in that case.

assumptions.assumption: A planned circuit lands only on busbars at its own nominal level (within 10%: 380/400/420 kV are one system, 60/63/66 kV another; 330/220 and 275/220 are not). A named station that holds no busbar at that level is not an exact match, and the endpoint falls back to the nearest major terminal AT that level. Sources that publish no voltage (RTE) get theirs from the best-weighted terminals first, then the same rule.
assumptions.basis: A branch between two levels shorts them without the transformer that really couples them, and pypsa derives x_pu from the bus voltage, so identical ohms carry (400/110)^2 = 13x less flow between two 110 kV busbars than between two 400 kV ones. Once the candidate floor followed the monitoring floor to 60 kV, a soft preference for the right level was not enough: 62 register sub-branches at 220-750 kV were built between two 110/132/60 kV busbars and relieved nothing, 70% of Norway's 420 kV licensed sub-branches landed on 132 kV busbars, and 55 380/400 kV schemes whose named station holds only a 110 kV busbar were dropped outright.
assumptions.bias: A scheme with no same-level terminal within its search radius is unresolved rather than misplaced, which understates plan relief for that scheme; it is counted (exact_refused_wrong_level, unresolved_endpoint).

assumptions.assumption: One RTE renewal work uprates exactly one existing French circuit - the most probable candidate span by w_start x w_end - and never a planned or foreign one.
assumptions.basis: A renewal replaces one conductor. Uplifting the whole candidate cross-product meant 471 works uprated 249 distinct spans, up to 8 circuits per work, roughly doubling credited French thermal capability - including a Spanish planned sub-branch raised by a French work.
assumptions.bias: Where a work genuinely re-conductors several spans, only one is credited. Understates French capability.

assumptions.assumption: An external corridor contributes at most one AC branch per bus pair per run.
assumptions.basis: The NVE licensing register and RTE Cart'Elec publish one licensed line as many features - '420 kV Lyse-Fagrafjell' alone is 36 - and the loader never fed its own output back into the parallel-circuit guard. 711 candidates became 924 branches on 369 pairs, worst case 33 parallel circuits totalling 27,810 MVA for a 3,000 MVA double circuit.
assumptions.bias: A genuine double circuit is modelled as one. Understates plan relief on those corridors.

assumptions.assumption: Where the source publishes no voltage, the branch takes the LOWER of its two ends' highest-weighted terminal voltages.
assumptions.basis: RTE Cart'Elec states no voltage at all. Taking the maximum across every candidate handed the branch the largest rating any candidate could justify - a 225 kV corridor typed 400 kV carries 1,787 MVA instead of about 500.
assumptions.bias: Conservative. May under-rate a genuine 400 kV work.

assumptions.assumption: Only connected components of at least 50 buses are screened. Every run report carries the count of buses, lines and transformers this excludes.
assumptions.basis: Screening a severed OSM fragment standalone produces nonsense. At the 60 kV floor this excludes roughly 9,200 spans and 9,700 buses (per-run counts are published in every run report as lines_dropped_below_floor and buses_below_floor), which previously happened with no count published anywhere.
assumptions.bias: Those branches are absent from the screen entirely. Islands above the floor carry their own area label rather than being pooled under 'Continental'. Sardinia is screened; Corsica is selected but currently produces NO results, because none of the TYNDP generation or demand weight lands on its buses - every run report says so ('skipped: no injection patterns') rather than leaving it silently absent.

assumptions.assumption: A corridor carrying n circuits is modelled as n parallel branches of rating/n and impedance xn, so a single contingency takes a single circuit.
assumptions.basis: The corridor used to be ONE branch, so its outage removed every circuit at once - a TPL-001 P7 common-structure event, not N-1, though every result was labelled N-1. It also broke comparability, because whether a double circuit is drawn as one way or two is an OpenStreetMap convention, not a grid property: 5% of Norway's multi-circuit backbone is bundled against 45% of GB's and 56% of Finland's, and a bundled corridor came out with 1.78x the headroom of the same line drawn as two ways. Splitting leaves the corridor's aggregate rating and admittance exactly as they were.
assumptions.bias: None known between countries; this removes a bias that favoured countries whose contributors bundle circuits. Common-tower double-circuit outages are still NOT taken, so corridors where both circuits share towers are screened optimistically against that event.

assumptions.assumption: Branches are monitored down to 60 kV, but contingencies are taken only on 220 kV and above (plus all transformers). Results are published in two tiers - transmission at 220 kV and above, sub-transmission below it - and never pooled.
assumptions.basis: A 90 kV circuit tripping is a local event; a 90 kV circuit is still worth watching under a backbone outage. Screening 73k outages against 73k monitored branches is roughly ten times the work for little screening value.
assumptions.bias: Understates stress on sub-transmission caused by sub-transmission outages. Backbone N-1 is unaffected.

assumptions.assumption: An RTE renewal work raises the existing circuit's thermal rating by 30%.
assumptions.basis: Reconductoring an existing corridor with modern conductor gives roughly +20-40% with larger conventional conductor and up to about 2x with HTLS/ACCC. RTE publishes no rating for these works, so the low-middle of the conventional range is used. A renewal replaces a circuit, so it is modelled as an uplift, never as an added parallel branch.
assumptions.bias: If RTE uses HTLS the uplift is understated, and French capability with it.

assumptions.assumption: French works take their voltage from the substations their endpoints resolve to.
assumptions.basis: RTE's SDDR publishes no voltage for any work. The same endpoint fallback is used for register schemes whose name carries no kV.
assumptions.bias: Neutral, but wrong endpoints would give a wrong voltage class and so a wrong typed rating.

assumptions.assumption: French works commission in 2030 (the 2030 works programme) or 2040 (the SDDR new-lines set).
assumptions.basis: RTE's own tileset naming. RTE publishes no commissioning year per work.
assumptions.bias: Coarse. Works inside the 2030 programme that slip past 2030 are modelled as delivered too early.

assumptions.assumption: A consented Norwegian line commissions 5 years after 2026; one still in licensing, 10 years after.
assumptions.basis: NVE publishes a licensing stage, not a date. The brackets are Norwegian consenting-to-energisation lead times, deliberately coarse rather than tuned.
assumptions.bias: Either direction per line. Consented lines that are already under construction arrive later here than in reality.

assumptions.assumption: A scheme with no published service year is admitted at the final horizon only (2040).
assumptions.basis: 462 line-like schemes carry no date. Dropping them made them invisible; dating them earlier would invent delivery.
assumptions.bias: Conservative before 2040: earlier horizons show less plan relief than may be real.

assumptions.assumption: Where a plan names a place rather than a substation, the circuit is split across the two or three plausible major terminals, with admittance and rating divided by weight.
assumptions.basis: Requiring an exact station match at both ends dropped 29% of line-like schemes, which understated plan relief in one direction.
assumptions.bias: This is an expected network, not a scenario ensemble. A real build lands the whole circuit on one terminal, and a fan creates a path between its own candidates that no single realisation has.

assumptions.assumption: A substation that does not exist yet is placed at the settlement it is named after.
assumptions.basis: A new station cannot be matched to OpenStreetMap because it is not built, but plans name it after its location - "New Zeebrugge", "UW Leoben (new)", "TS Crkvicko Polje (ME), new". 216 of 230 such endpoints carry a usable place name, and the settlement is the best available position. The endpoint resolver then snaps from there to the plausible major terminals nearby.
assumptions.bias: The position is the settlement, not the site: a station built on the edge of a district lands at the district centre here. Corridor lengths near it are approximate.

assumptions.assumption: Endpoint names are matched after stripping commentary, page references, our own annotations, articles and prepositions, and station-type words in each language; Greek and Cyrillic are transliterated to Latin on both sides with one fixed scheme; digits stay part of a name (TEC-1 is not TEC-2) while voltages do not. An endpoint cell is also tried segment by segment (via-clauses cut, dash- and slash-separated alternatives, its own '(DE)'-style country hint). When several catalogue names all contain the endpoint name, the most specific is taken rather than none. The unmatched end of a scheme whose other end is known is retried against stations within one corridor length (at most 300 km) of that end, accepting only spelling variants of the same stem (Lanesboro / Lanesborough, Toivila / Toivilan). A border crossing named as an endpoint is a border point, not a failed station match; a station in a neighbouring country is accepted only when the endpoint text itself points there.
assumptions.basis: Plans write endpoints as prose, in twenty languages and three alphabets. Before transliteration no Greek, Bulgarian or Serbian station could match at all (their OSM names are in native script); "Subestação de Armamar" never matched "Armamar" because of the "de"; and the uniqueness margin rejected exact matches whenever a longer sibling name existed.
assumptions.bias: Over-stripping could match the wrong station. Matching stays on a high fuzzy threshold with a margin over the runner-up, the near pass adds a same-stem test and a distance cap, and every match carries its rule in the provenance text.

assumptions.assumption: When a plan names a station that holds no busbar at the scheme's voltage, the scheme creates one: a new busbar at that station at the scheme's voltage, coupled to the station's highest existing level by a transformer typed from the v23 transformer table (per-class medians). The same rule serves a place-anchored endpoint with no station at the scheme's level within 25 km: the nearest existing station receives the new busbar. Every scheme landing there shares it.
assumptions.basis: "380-kV-Leitung Trumau - Hessenberg" builds 380 kV at Hessenberg, which is 110/220 kV today. 111 schemes at 2040 were dropped for want of a same-level terminal within 15 km and others quietly landed on a different station up to 15 km away. Substation extension to a new level is what such plans describe.
assumptions.bias: The new busbar's coupling transformer is typed, not sourced, so its impedance is a class median; the busbar's position is the existing station's. Where a plan really builds a wholly new station elsewhere, the circuit lands one station too close to the old one.

assumptions.assumption: A scheme's voltage is read from its name first, then from the register's own voltage field, then from a NESO circuit id suffix (BODE_400), then from the matched endpoint stations.
assumptions.basis: 73 schemes were dropped for 'no voltage' while the register row beside them stated one; 55 of them GB Beyond-2030 reinforcements.
assumptions.bias: None beyond the field's own accuracy; the source of the voltage is recorded per branch.

assumptions.assumption: Every planned circuit is typed with the median x/km, r/km and s_nom of its voltage class in the v23 backbone.
assumptions.basis: No promoter publishes impedances. Class medians are the only defensible typing without an asset register.
assumptions.bias: A heavier-than-median build is understated and vice versa.

assumptions.assumption: A DC link of 500 MW or more enters as a 1 GW converter-injection pattern, not a flow-carrying branch.
assumptions.basis: Per GW the AC-flow consequence of a schedule swing and of a full-import outage is the same linear pattern.
assumptions.bias: Conservative where embedded HVDC parallels AC: the link provides no relief in the default columns. The 'with DC redispatch' view is the labelled exception below.

assumptions.assumption: The 'with DC redispatch' view raises a branch's headroom by the single most helpful HVDC link redispatched to its full rating at that branch's binding case.
assumptions.basis: HVDC setpoints are controllable within post-fault timescales, and relieving paralleled AC corridors is a stated purpose of the planned links. The link's converter pattern response is the same physics the swing screen already computes.
assumptions.bias: Optimistic per branch, in three stated ways: one link per branch but every branch assumes ITS best link (no shared dispatch), relief is evaluated at the unrelieved binding case only (a nearly-as-severe second case with no DC leverage narrows the true gain), and full rating assumes no concurrent market schedule. The default view keeps the no-relief limit.

assumptions.assumption: Refurbishments, uprates and series devices are not added as new circuits, in any of the plans' languages (repotenciación, renovación, rekonstrueerimine, verzwaren, Kabel REI, power line renewal, modernizare, major maintenance ...). A work on a corridor that already carries a circuit, whose wording does not say 'new circuit' in any language, is credited the same way a refurbishment is - as a rating uplift on the existing circuit - rather than dropped.
assumptions.basis: Adding refurbishments created phantom parallel corridors (Spanish 'repotenciación' alone put 41 uprating works on the map as second circuits); dropping unspecific corridor works hid 372 schemes at 2040 that plainly change the corridor. Note that 'reinforcement' is NOT filtered: in TSO usage a named reinforcement is new build.
assumptions.bias: A refurbishment, uprating or unspecific corridor scheme credits the existing corridor between its two ends with the same x1.3 conductor uplift as an RTE renewal: the corridor is the shortest chain of existing spans, in kilometres, at the level the work runs at, capped at 3x the drawn length plus 40 km; one circuit per span unless the wording says both, and a span is never uplifted twice across sources (a second row on an already-credited corridor is recorded as the same work). Conservative where the work is in fact a second circuit; the multilingual 'second circuit' wording catches the ones that say so. Series devices remain uncredited: their benefit is dispatch-dependent, which this screen does not model.

assumptions.assumption: The voltage at which a refurbishment or uprating is looked for is the level of the EXISTING circuit: the lowest figure the wording quotes ('275 kV to 400 kV' works on a 275 kV circuit), else the highest level the two named stations share, else any other quoted figure; levels are tried in that order until one yields a corridor of existing spans.
assumptions.basis: Half the NESO reconductoring schemes quote no voltage at all ('Replace the conductors on the existing circuit between Feckenham and Hams Hall'). Taking each station's lowest busbar found a 66 kV Feckenham and a 132 kV Hams Hall with no span between them; taking a voltage upgrade's target level searched a network that does not exist yet. Reconductoring named between two transmission stations is transmission work.
assumptions.bias: A voltage upgrade is credited as a x1.3 uplift of the lower level's circuit, not as the new higher-voltage circuit it will become: conservative on capacity, and the corridor keeps the old level's impedance. Where two stations share several levels and the wording says nothing, the highest is taken; a sub-transmission reconductoring between two 400 kV stations would be credited one level too high.

assumptions.assumption: When no continuous chain of existing spans joins the two ends of a refurbishment at any of its candidate levels, the spans lying under the promoter's drawn route are the ones reconductored: existing spans within 1 km of the route, each at least 60% inside that corridor, together covering at least 30% of the route, at the scheme's level or, failing that, any transmission level (>= 220 kV).
assumptions.basis: The v23 graph is not continuous everywhere: Walham 400 kV carries no span towards Feckenham although the A586 circuit runs there, and Kincardine North 400 kV carries no span at all. Twelve schemes drawn from NESO's own route shapefiles (Feckenham-Walham, Feckenham-Minety, Spennymoor-Stella West, Bramford-Braintree-Rayleigh ...) found no chain for that reason alone.
assumptions.bias: The spans under the route are uplifted but the gap in the graph is not closed, so the corridor stays as broken in the screen as it was before. A route drawn schematically (a straight line between two stations) rarely stays within 1 km of the real spans and is rarely credited this way. Where a voltage upgrade is credited at the tier level, the circuit keeps its present voltage and impedance.

assumptions.assumption: Every HVDC link of 500 MW or more in the network at a horizon - existing, under construction, in a register or in the TYNDP portfolio - is a controllable element. For each scenario transfer pattern the links' set-points are chosen together, within each link's rating, to reduce the excess utilisation of the transmission-tier branches above the 12 GW headroom line (a linear programme per pattern), under two hard rules: a branch above that line may never be pushed below it, and a branch already below it may not be made more than a quarter worse. A link's share of each GW of transfer is bounded so that it reaches its rating at the 12 GW line and never beyond (a 2 GW embedded link carries at most 2/12 GW per GW). A link is used only where a GW of it buys more than 0.02 per unit of relief. The AC flows the screen reports include those set-points, held post-fault. An embedded link (both converters inside the synchronous area) may use its full rating; an interconnector or offshore landing only half.
assumptions.basis: Embedded HVDC is built precisely for controllable, separable relief of the AC network - the Eastern Green Links, SuedLink and Ultranet are operated for constraint management. Until v4.7 the screen modelled only the stress a link imposes and gave it no relief. A first formulation that minimised the single worst utilisation loaded thousands of other circuits (stressed >=220 kV circuits at 2040 rose from 3,686 to 5,222 Europe-wide) and was replaced by this relief-only form. Interconnector schedules are market-driven; only countertrading and redispatch move them, so half the rating is taken as available.
assumptions.bias: Optimistic where the operator would not run a link for constraint relief, and for interconnectors the half-rating share is a round assumption in both directions. The 12 GW line, the quarter and the 0.02 per unit per GW are ours (a tenth halved the relief the existing GB links could give; the quarter recovers most of it). Bounding a link by its full rating per GW - the first build - implied a 2 GW link carrying 24 GW at the 12 GW line, relieved corridors about ten times too much and failed the GB direction gate. Every new link also adds a 1 GW converter-swing stress pattern, so the headline worst-of-both column grows redder around new landings even as the bulk-transfer column is relieved. Post-fault the set-points are held, which is conservative: real schemes re-dispatch after a fault (the 'with DC redispatch' view keeps that single-link counterfactual). Relief is measured on pre-fault flows per pattern; a post-fault flow can still worsen for some contingencies.

assumptions.assumption: An HVDC link whose source states no rating is given one by class: 2 GW at 500 kV and above, 1.4 GW at 300-499 kV, 2 GW for a link named as a 2 GW-class scheme (Eastern Green Link, Sea Link, SuedLink, Ultranet), else 1 GW. Register and TYNDP links land on the matched station, else on the nearest >=220 kV station within 40 km of the drawn end; an end with nothing in reach is offshore or abroad and the link enters as a landing infeed. A TYNDP DC study corridor (an area) is read along its long axis. The same link listed by several sources counts once (OSM before register before TYNDP).
assumptions.basis: The register's HVDC rows quote a capacity in 3 of 24 cases and the TYNDP portfolio quotes none; the DC voltage class is stated far more often and tracks rating closely in practice.
assumptions.bias: A defaulted rating can be wrong by a factor of two either way (a 320 kV link may be 700 MW or 1.4 GW); every defaulted figure is flagged in the link's provenance. A corridor's long axis may end at the wrong station when the area is broad.

assumptions.assumption: A coded NESO 'future circuit' (BEDD_400, HUCS_400, SW_E1a/b/c, AC6, INTOG, HND_CS_FW, HND_PA ...) with a drawn end more than 40 km from any station at its level, or longer than 250 km, is an offshore element: an HVDC link (2 GW class when coded 400 kV, 1.4 GW when 275 kV) landing at the station it reaches, never an AC circuit. A future circuit landing offshore generation (one country, one landing) is a stress pattern only; it is not dispatched for relief. Coded 132 kV offshore connections are a wind farm's own export cable and are left out.
assumptions.basis: NESO publishes its offshore network design as bare coded lines without a technology field. Read as 400 kV AC with new stations at their sea ends, they formed an AC mesh at sea bypassing the B6 boundary: 67 GB circuits became stressed pre-fault and Alverdiscott's 400 kV feed jumped from 4 to 520 MW per GW. No AC circuit of that length is built at sea; these are the HVDC bootstraps and wind connections of the Holistic Network Design.
assumptions.bias: A long onshore future circuit (none is known) would be wrongly read as HVDC. Landing points are the nearest station within 40 km of the drawn end, which may not be the design's.

assumptions.assumption: A converter-swing stress pattern is per GW of swing, but a link can swing at most its rating. Where the swing that would saturate a branch exceeds the link's rating, that link cannot saturate that branch and the figure is not counted as DC-swing stress.
assumptions.basis: With every planned HVDC link carrying a converter pattern, a branch that saturated at 8 GW of swing under a 1 GW link was coloured as if 8 GW could happen; the headline grew redder with each link added (GB 2040 with plans: 275 -> 467 pre-fault stressed circuits, all DC-mechanism).
assumptions.bias: A link's rating is the cap for a single link; two links swinging together are not combined, so joint events are understated. Links with a defaulted rating carry that default's uncertainty into the cap.

assumptions.assumption: A TYNDP project drawn between generalised points is attached in three steps: the nearest terminals at its voltage within 15 km of the drawn end; failing that, within 40 km, fanned over the nearest major substations by distance; failing that, the nearest >=220 kV station within 40 km receives a new busbar at the project's voltage, coupled by a typed transformer.
assumptions.basis: The portfolio draws many projects between a region's centre or a substation that does not exist yet: the North South Interconnector ends where Turleenan 400 kV will be, on a 275 kV network, and 19 of 51 eligible AC projects at 2040 were dropped as unresolved. The point of the portfolio is the relief the projects bring; a dropped project brings none.
assumptions.bias: The landing may be a neighbour of the intended substation and the new busbar's transformer is typed, not sourced; corridor lengths near a fanned end are approximate.

assumptions.assumption: A planned work published only as an AREA - an RTE 400 kV programme phase named after two stations ('CHAINGY-DAMBRON'), or a TYNDP AC study corridor - enters as one circuit: between the two named stations, or along the area's long axis to the nearest transmission stations (searched within 40 km). Voltage from the source, else 400 kV; year from the source, else 2035 for an RTE Phase 1 zone and 2040 for a TYNDP corridor with no date.
assumptions.basis: These plans refer to major upgrades or interconnections whose route is not yet chosen; leaving them out understated the planned network exactly where the largest works are. RTE's phases and the TYNDP corridors both name their ends or span a region whose extremities are the obvious terminals.
assumptions.bias: The circuit's length and terminals are approximate, so its impedance and the corridor it parallels may be off; the commissioning years for undated works are ours.

assumptions.assumption: A reinforcement area with no named ends ('MASSIF CENTRAL', 'HTLS in Lyonnais', 'Limitations removal on the Italian-Slovenian border', PST installations) is read as reinforcement of the network inside it: every existing span at the programme's level lying at least 60% inside the polygon takes the x1.3 conductor uplift, once - the 400 kV spans for an RTE 400 kV programme phase, the >=220 kV spans for a TYNDP area. Synchronisation programmes are not read as uplifts.
assumptions.basis: Such areas say the network there is reinforced without saying how; an uprating of what exists is the conservative reading and the same figure the renewal works already carry.
assumptions.bias: A phase-shifter or a synchronisation project changes power flow control, not thermal rating; crediting it as a rating uplift is a proxy. Spans just outside the polygon get nothing.

assumptions.assumption: When a planned circuit's drawn end lies where no station at the scheme's level exists within reach and the plan names none, the plan builds a new station there: a busbar at the drawn end, at the scheme's voltage, shared by every scheme drawn to within about 1.5 km of it. It has no transformer, there being nothing existing to couple to.
assumptions.basis: Loch Buidhe is a new 400 kV switching station in Sutherland at the meeting point of three NESO circuits; no 400 kV station lies within 40 km. Without the rule every circuit into it was dropped as unresolved and the through-path they form did not exist in the model.
assumptions.bias: A circuit into a new station that no other planned circuit reaches is a radial dead end: it carries no flow, so it appears screened but unexposed rather than absent. The station's position is the drawn end, which for a schematic line is approximate.
